title: My, your, our: -ni, -si, -mme, -nne
summary: A possessive ending is a short ending on the noun that tells us its owner. For these regular singular nouns, attach -ni, -si, -mme, or -nne to the complete basic noun.
objectives: Attach -ni, -si, -mme, or -nne to match the owner.
Recognise the pattern, then produce it with the supporting words shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: A possessive ending is a short ending on the noun that tells us its owner. For these regular singular nouns, attach -ni, -si, -mme, or -nne to the complete basic noun.

Minun pallo + -ni = minun palloni; sinun kirja + -si = sinun kirjasi; meidän auto + -mme = meidän automme; teidän pallo + -nne = teidän pallonne. Keep the consonant doubles in -mme and -nne. The noun names one thing even when several people own it.
keyPoints: Practise one singular possessed thing with the supporting forms shown.

steps: Attach it to the complete basic word pallo (“ball”): pallo + -ni = palloni.
Kirja (“book”) + -si = kirjasi; keep the final a before the ending.
Meidän (“our”) chooses -mme. Several owners can own one car.
Auto (“car”) + -mme = automme; keep both m letters.
Pallo (“ball”) + -nne = pallonne; keep both n letters, distinct from -ni.
Minun again chooses -ni, independently of the noun.
Kissa (“cat”) + -ni = kissani; retain the complete basic word.
Sinun again chooses -si for one owner addressed as “you”.
Teidän (“your”, a group) chooses -nne: omena (“apple”) + -nne = omenanne. The owner determines the ending, not the noun.

commonMistakes: In these standard-written personal-owner phrases, keep the noun ending as well as the owner pronoun: minun palloni, rather than minun pallo.
Match the ending to the owner: -ni for minun, -si for sinun, -mme for meidän, and -nne for teidän.
Keep both consonants in -mme and -nne; the noun can still name one thing with several owners.
